intro: Castlewellan Forest Park, in County Down, keeps its oldest conifers in the walled Annesley Garden and arboretum. A giant sequoia planted as a sapling in 1856 has grown nineteen trunks and was Northern Ireland's Tree of the Year in 2018. Near the entrance path a pair of redwoods faces each other, one of them named the most gigantic in Ulster. The garden also bred the golden Leyland cypress sold as Castlewellan Gold. Entry is free on foot.
meta_description: Castlewellan Forest Park, County Down: a 19-trunk sequoia from 1856, Ulster's biggest redwood and the first Castlewellan Gold. Free on foot.
question_meta: Castlewellan's remarkable trees are 19th-century giant sequoias in the Annesley Garden, one with 19 trunks, Northern Ireland's Tree of the Year 2018.
question_answer: Castlewellan's best-known tree is the multi-stemmed giant sequoia in the walled Annesley Garden, planted as a sapling in 1856 and grown into nineteen trunks. Northern Ireland voted it Tree of the Year in 2018. The oldest documented trees in the park are its sequoias, more than 160 years old.
question_context: The park's giant sequoias grew from seed William Lobb brought from California in 1853 for the Veitch nurseries, planted out as saplings in 1856. The multi-stemmed tree is the best recorded of them. The 5th Earl Annesley photographed it in 1871 at fifteen years old, and its lower branches have since layered and rooted until it stands on nineteen trunks. Near the arboretum's entrance path, beside formal steps, two more redwoods face each other across the path. Northern Ireland's Forest Service book calls one of them the most gigantic of Ulster's redwoods, and gives one of the pair a girth of 22 feet 2 inches without making clear which. Their own planting date is not recorded. The garden is also where the park's director, John Keown, spotted the golden seedling that became the hedge plant Castlewellan Gold, named in 1963; whether the original still stands has not been confirmed recently. A California nutmeg here is called the tallest of its kind in Britain and Ireland, on measurements from 1982, and nobody has published where it stands. Recent sightings of any of them are welcome.

faq.a: Free on foot. Cars pay a charge at the park; the amount is on the nidirect page for Castlewellan Forest Park.

faq.q: When is the Annesley Garden open?
faq.a: Daily from 10 am until sunset. The walled garden is reached through the forest park.

faq.q: How old are the sequoias at Castlewellan?
faq.a: More than 160 years. They grew from seed brought from California in 1853 and were planted out as saplings in 1856.

faq.q: Is the original Castlewellan Gold still there?
faq.a: Probably, but we have no recent dated sighting. It is said to stand in the ornamental gardens near the Heron Fountain; if you see it, tell us.

faq.q: How do you get to Castlewellan Forest Park by bus?
faq.a: Ulsterbus services between Newcastle and Newry stop in Castlewellan village, about 1.5 km from the park entrance.

trees.name: The Castlewellan Great Redwoods

location.address: Annesley Garden (walled garden and arboretum), Castlewellan Forest Park, Castlewellan BT31 9BU

trees.story:
Northern Ireland's Forest Service book on remarkable trees calls one of these the most gigantic of all Ulster's redwoods. It stands beside formal steps near the entrance path of the Castlewellan arboretum, and directly opposite, across the path, stands another giant that the book says is nearly as tall and measures 22 feet 2 inches, about 6.75 metres, round at chest height. The text does not make clear which of the two that girth belongs to, so we give it to the pair rather than guess. No height in metres has been published.

The park's giant sequoias came from seed William Lobb brought from California in 1853 and were planted out as saplings in 1856. Nobody has written down when this pair went in, so their age here is the age of the park's sequoias in general, more than 160 years, not a date for these two. They may be younger.

The path runs between them, so you meet the pair before you meet anything else in the arboretum. That is the whole visit, and it is enough.

We found no dated report on the pair from the last few years, and our pin comes from a photographer's position in 2012, so it is close but not exact. If you see them, tell us. The park is free on foot, with a charge for cars, and the Annesley Garden is open daily from 10 am until sunset.

trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise them as two huge redwoods facing each other across the path, beside the formal steps near the arboretum's entrance path. They tower over everything around them.
trees.pin_source: Geograph/Commons photo 'Giant Redwoods in the Castlewellan Castle Arboretum' (Eric Jones, 2012) geotagged 54.26534, -5.95243 (10 m precision, subject heading 67 degrees); consistent with the book's 'beside formal steps near the entrance path'. Not a pin on one named crown.
trees.verify_notes: Northern Ireland's Remarkable Trees (Forest Service book, remarkabletrees.org, read via Wayback 2025-12 copy): 'the most gigantic of them all' of the Ulster redwoods is in the arboretum at Castlewellan, standing beside formal steps near the entrance path. Opposite is another giant, the Sierra Redwood, nearly as tall and measuring 22 ft 2 in (about 675 cm) at chest height; unclear from the text which one is the 22 ft 2 in tree, so girth_cm left empty. Folded as one ensemble with one place to stand. No metre height stated. Age: Castlewellan sequoias grown from William Lobb seed introduced 1853 and planted as saplings 1856 (Wikipedia, Down News); the great redwoods' own planting date not stated, so age is 'over 160 years' only as the park's sequoias, not claimed for this pair specifically. Alive: no dated post-2022 report seen for this pair; flagged. The book calls it the biggest in Ulster but gives no champion record figure; do not write a superlative beyond 'the book names it the most gigantic of Ulster's redwoods'.

trees.name: The Castlewellan Multi-Stemmed Sequoia

location.address: Walled Annesley Garden, Castlewellan Forest Park, Castlewellan BT31 9BU

trees.story:
This giant sequoia has nineteen trunks, a form its admirers say is rarely seen outside the wild. Instead of one column it grew a family. Its lower branches swept sideways, bowed to the ground and layered, rooting where they touched and sending up new stems, until one tree became a small grove of itself.

Its start is unusually well recorded. William Lobb brought the seed from California in 1853 for the Veitch nurseries, and this tree went into the walled garden at Castlewellan as a sapling in 1856. In 1871 the 5th Earl Annesley photographed it at fifteen years old, so there is a picture of this tree as a teenager. It is about 170 years old now.

In 2018 Northern Ireland voted it Tree of the Year, with 912 votes in the Woodland Trust contest. Plenty of trees here are bigger. This is the one whose shape is the point.

Nobody has published its girth or height, and we found no dated report since the award and the Forest Service book, so a recent photograph is welcome. Our pin is the centre of the walled Annesley Garden, not the tree, though nineteen trunks beside a path are hard to miss. The park is free on foot, with a charge for cars, and the garden opens daily from 10 am until sunset.

trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its 19 separate trunks and branches that sweep sideways and bow to the ground. It stands beside a path in the walled Annesley Garden; our pin marks the garden, not the tree.
trees.pin_source: Walled garden centre (Heron Fountain area, 54.2651, -5.9506); no source gives a coordinate for this crown.
trees.verify_notes: Northern Ireland Tree of the Year 2018 (Woodland Trust, 912 votes; Down News 17 Oct 2018 and Redwood World). Planted as a sapling in 1856 (Redwood World quoting the nomination; a photograph of it by the 5th Earl Annesley in 1871 shows it at fifteen years old) from seed brought from California by William Lobb in 1853 for Veitch Nurseries. 19 trunks, 'a form rarely seen other than in the wild'; the Remarkable Trees book describes the branches layering and forming new trees. Down News says 'over 160 years old'. Same tree as Wikipedia's 'one tree has developed 19 separate trunks'. Girth and height not published. Alive: ToY 2018 and the book; no recent dated report seen; flagged.

trees.name: The Original Castlewellan Gold

location.address: Ornamental gardens, Castlewellan Forest Park, Castlewellan BT31 9BU

trees.story:
Thousands of golden hedges in Northern Ireland began as cuttings from one odd seedling in these gardens. It was a mutant, a Leyland cypress with golden foliage, and the park's director, John Keown, spotted it, nurtured it and sheltered it. In 1963 it was named Cupressus macrocarpa 'Keownii', though later botanists class it as a hybrid that arose beside a Nootka cypress, not a pure Monterey cypress. Under the name Castlewellan Gold its cuttings were planted as hedges right across Ulster.

The original is young by the standards of this map. It was a seedling in the early 1960s, so it is about sixty years old at most. It is here because it is the parent of a hedge plant that many people walk past every day without knowing where it came from.

We have to be honest about two things. We do not know for certain that the original still stands. The sources that name it are older, and the most recent mention we found is a 2026 visitor guide listing it among the park's champions, which is not the same as somebody checking. And our pin marks the Heron Fountain area of the ornamental gardens, where it is said to grow, not the tree itself. Without a label it may be hard to tell from its neighbours.

If you have seen it recently, a photograph and a word would settle both questions. The park is free on foot, with a charge for cars.

trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its golden foliage, the parent of every Castlewellan Gold hedge. It is said to stand in the ornamental gardens near the Heron Fountain, and without a sign it may be hard to tell from its neighbours.
trees.pin_source: Approximate: 'ornamental gardens' per Wikipedia; sources elsewhere say two parent trees stand in the lee of the Heron Fountain area (search snippet, unseen on a fetched page). Pin set at the Heron Fountain.
trees.verify_notes: Two sources: Wikipedia (Castlewellan Gold Leyland cypress developed in the park from a mutant, selected by park director John Keown, named Cupressus macrocarpa 'Keownii' in 1963; original specimen in the ornamental gardens) and the Remarkable Trees book (the original is the source of the thousands of cuttings planted as hedges across Ulster; spotted as a seedling, nurtured and sheltered). Hybrid, not pure macrocarpa (Conifer Society / RBG Victoria entries say it arose beside Nootka cypress). Tree is about 60-65 years old at most (seedling stage in the early 1960s); no girth. Alive now unconfirmed: no dated report; is the original still standing? Flagged, must be checked before writing. Pin not on a crown.

trees.name: The Castlewellan Nutmeg Tree

location.address: Annesley Garden / arboretum, Castlewellan Forest Park, Castlewellan BT31 9BU

trees.story:
Castlewellan's district council calls this the tallest California nutmeg in Britain and Ireland, one of 47 champion trees in the park's collection. The claim is undated, and the measurements we can find are old. Bean's Trees and Shrubs records it at 66 feet tall and 10.75 feet round in 1982, about 20 metres by 3.3 metres, up from 56 feet in 1976. A later record from 2000 gives a trunk diameter of 123 cm. Nobody has published a figure since, so read the crown as the council's and the numbers as forty years old.

Between 1976 and 1982 it put on ten feet in height, which is the last growth anyone recorded.

Here is the problem with visiting it. No source we have read says where in the collection it stands. Our pin is the centre of the walled Annesley Garden, and we cannot tell you which tree to look for beyond its species. Its age is not documented either.

So this is a tree for someone who knows conifers, or who asks at the park. If you find it, tell us where it stands, and a photograph of the trunk would put it properly on the map. The park is free on foot, with a charge for cars, and the garden is open daily from 10 am until sunset.

trees.verify_notes: Newry, Mourne and Down District Council article: the Nutmeg Tree Torreya californica is 'the height champion in Britain and Ireland', one of 47 champion trees in the collection. Bean's Trees and Shrubs (Trees and Shrubs Online, fetched): Castlewellan 66 x 10.75 ft (1982), i.e. about 20 m tall and 328 cm girth in 1982 (earlier 56 x 10.25 ft in 1976). Gymnosperm Database: 123 cm dbh recorded in 2000 (status unknown). Figures are 1982, not current; the council champion claim is undated. Spot unknown: findability is weak (no recognition possible beyond the species).
